Presidential Gubernatorial President of AUN, Margee Ensign
Nigeria faces a critical moment in its political history and development trajectory. The giant of Africa in population and GDP, Nigeria is projected to be the third largest country in the world by 2050, surpassing the United States.
In less than two months, Nigerians will hold consequential elections. Nigeria is facing interconnected humanitarian crises of insecurity, economic hardship, increasing poverty and unemployment. The removal of fuel subsidies, economic mismanagement and corruption have compounded these problems.
Progress in reducing poverty and inequality, generating employment for an increasingly youthful population, and improving access to health care and education has stalled in the last decade. Close to 32 percent of children under five are stunted and will never reach their full cognitive and physical potential. An estimated 2 million children suffer from severe acute malnutrition. According to UNICEF over 20 million children are out of school. To Nigeria’s shame this is 15% of the global total.
Education is the foundation of a society. It is the engine of growth, employment, democracy, public health and gender equity. One presidential candidate has spent a lifetime supporting education. We worked at the university Atiku Abubakar founded, the American University of Nigeria (AUN). One was president for eight years; one was a faculty member and Vice-President of Safety and Security for thirteen years and one was a member of the AUN Board for twelve years. What attracted all of us was his vision of the university to be a development university.
AUN was founded on a different model of education– to prepare young people to address the country’s development challenges and built on the premise that education is most powerful when students gain deep knowledge and learn how to apply it. To build enterprises, develop innovative solutions to poverty and inequality, and to use technology to solve problems in their own communities.
AUN has lived the mission of a development university through some very difficult times in Northeast Nigeria. At the height of the Boko Haram crisis in Yola, Atiku Abubakar sent a note with these words: “Make sure no one in Yola goes hungry.” During this trying time, he supported the university’s efforts (students, faculty and staff) to feed and educate the 300,000 internally displaced people in the community. When we brought the Chibok students to AUN and did not have the funds for their housing, clothing and education, Atiku Abubakar and an American businessman, Robert Smith, supported all their expenses.
AUN established the lead in the region by remaining open. This would not have been possible without the intervention of AUN’s Founder, who supported the security measures that were implemented at the university as well as the surrounding communities.

His contribution was not only strategic, but also technological. He advised on the Monday morning program, Safiya, on Gotel Radio and TV, where information was broadcast to the region for a year on safety and security matters.
Atiku Abubakar’s contribution to safety and security included education. In the midst of the insurgency, AUN was able to serve the children of Yola and the surrounding areas by establishing the Feed and Read programme, which created distance between the young children and Boko Haram. This feeding not only helped the poor and impoverished and the IDP’s; it reduced the recruitment of young men into the ranks of the insurgents and bandits.
One child told us that it was either join Feed and Read or Boko Haram. When one university north of Yola was destroyed by Boko Haram , the Founder allowed their students to use AUN’s facilities assuring that they graduated on time
Building a successful university requires years of investment in people, facilities, faculty, technology, academic programmes, and institutional capacity. Because of his experience with American Peace Corps teachers as a child, he was favourably familiar with American educational models, arguably the world’s most effective. Atiku’s role in establishing AUN stands out because he directed his wealth toward a public purpose with consequences that can extend across generations: the education of young Nigerians and the strengthening of the country’s human capital.
At this critical moment in Nigeria’s history, it is important that the country understands his vision and accomplishments as we saw them during over a decade. Atiku Abubakar’s vision and investment in education reflect a sustained belief in the future and in the capacity of Nigerians to create it.
Perhaps the best summation of his contribution to education came from the U.S. Peace Corps. In 2011 he received the Peace Corps’ Harris Wofford Global Citizen Award.
“Atiku Abubakar has had a distinguished career in public service, private business, and philanthropy. Perhaps his most outstanding legacy was his founding and support of the American University of Nigeria, the outstanding private university in sub-Saharan Africa. No private businessman in Africa has worked harder for democracy or contributed more to the progress of higher education than Atiku Abubakar. And he himself acknowledges that one of the main reasons was the influence of his Peace Corps.”
While his place on the ballot is being contested, Nigerians should have the opportunity to vote for an education president, Atiku Abubakar.
Margee Ensign, a former President (vice-chancellor) of the American University of Nigeria, Yola, Ensign is currently a Senior Fellow at Bard College.
William Bertrand is Professor Emeritus at Tulane University.
Dr Lionel Rawlins is the National Security Advisor at St. Kitts.
Margee M. Ensign has been a university president for the past fifteen years, both in the United States, at Dickinson College, and in sub-Saharan Africa and Eastern Europe. She is currently a senior fellow at the Center for Civic Engagement at Bard College.
